eyebrow: Travel Like an Ang Thong Local · Updated 2026
intro: Ang Thong is a small town near Bangkok packed with beautiful temples, giant Buddhas and delightful oddities — from the gleaming golden Luang Pho Yai of Wat Muang rising out of the rice fields and the colossal reclining Buddha at Wat Khun Inthapramun, to the iron-robot house and the rare bodhi-wrapped chapel. We've gathered the 10 attractions visitors to Ang Thong talk about most, all in one place — and a single day's drive covers plenty of them.
chips: 🛕 Luang Pho Yai at Wat Muang — Thailand's biggest Buddha
🛌 Reclining Buddha of Wat Khun Inthapramun
🌳 Bodhi-wrapped chapel at Wat Sang Kratai

blocks.html:
Ang Thong is a small province on the central plains, only about an hour and a half to two hours from Bangkok. Its charm is that everything sits close together and most of it is free to enter, so you can take the day at your own pace, ticking off one stop at a time. In the morning, pay respects to Luang Pho Yai at Wat Muang, towering over the rice fields on the Wiset Chai Chan side. Late morning, swing toward Pho Thong for the giant reclining Buddha at Wat Khun Inthapramun and Kham Yat Palace out in the fields. In the afternoon, drop by the kid-favorite Ban Hun Lek iron-robot house in town, then wrap up at the century-old San Chao Rong Thong Market on the Noi River, snacking on traditional Thai sweets among the old wooden shophouses. An Ang Thong trip ends up an easygoing outing that suits merit-makers, photographers and families alike.

Several places on this list are icons of the province. The true headliner is Phra Buddha Maha Nawamin Sakyamuni Sri Wiset Chai Chan — Luang Pho Yai of Wat Muang — with a lap width of around 63 meters and a height of around 95 meters, the largest seated Buddha in Thailand, its brilliant gold visible from far away. Wat Khun Inthapramun has an open-air reclining Buddha around 50 meters long, an ancient image that ranks among the country's largest. At Pa Mok there's a Sukhothai-era stucco reclining Buddha beside the Chao Phraya, with the legend of the talking reclining Buddha. Wat Sang Kratai has an old ordination hall entirely embraced by the roots of a great bodhi tree, now one of the most atmospheric photo spots around. And Ang Thong is home to the Ekkarat drum-making village, the biggest and best known in Thailand. Tick them all off and you'll understand why this little province is a merit-making destination people return to without ever tiring of it.

blocks.name: Wat Muang (Luang Pho Yai — Phra Buddha Maha Nawamin Sakyamuni Sri Wiset Chai Chan)
blocks.area: Hua Taphan, Wiset Chai Chan District
blocks.signature: Thailand's largest seated Buddha, brilliant gold in the middle of the rice fields, lap width around 63 m and height around 95 m + model Hell-and-Heaven grounds and the Crystal Vihara
blocks.descHtml:
If you come to Ang Thong and skip Wat Muang, locals will tell you that you haven't really arrived. The main event everyone comes for is “Luang Pho Yai,” or Phra Buddha Maha Nawamin Sakyamuni Sri Wiset Chai Chan — the largest seated Buddha in Thailand, in the subduing-Mara posture, with a lap width of around 63 meters and rising nearly 95 meters from base to crown, roughly the height of a thirty-plus-story building. Painted a brilliant gold and standing tall in the middle of the rice fields, it can be seen from far away. Many visitors agree that standing beneath the actual statue makes you feel instantly small. The temple suits merit-makers, families bringing older relatives, and anyone who loves photographing giant landmarks.

Beyond the big Buddha, there's plenty more to see around the temple. Don't miss Phra Wihan Kaew, the Crystal Vihara (Rattanapram–Suwannapal), whose glittering interior gets rave mentions in many reviews, and the model “Hell and Heaven” grounds around the temple, with towering hungry-ghost statues and punishment scenes drawn from the Tripitaka. Some visitors find them fairly frightening and realistic, so time it carefully if you bring small children. There are also a Chinese deity zone, statues of Thai literary figures, and an ordination hall ringed by huge pink lotus petals to photograph.

Budget-wise it's very easy, since the temple charges no entry fee — just donations as you see fit, plus amulet-rental stalls. The most popular belief is to walk up and touch the fingertips of Luang Pho Yai while praying for career and money luck, which is why the place is packed almost every holiday. The temple is open around 06:00–18:00, located at Mu 6, Hua Taphan, Wiset Chai Chan District, roughly 8 kilometers west of Ang Thong town and about a 1.5-hour drive from Bangkok.

A few things to know: the plaza around the Buddha is open ground in full sun, and it gets very hot from late morning through the afternoon — bring an umbrella, hat, drinking water and sunscreen. Dress modestly, as this is a temple. Parking is spacious enough for tour buses, and there are restaurants and souvenir shops out front. For the best light on the golden Buddha against the sky, come early morning or evening, when the atmosphere is just right and it's less crowded than midday.
mustOrder: Touch Luang Pho Yai's fingertips and make a wish
The glittering Crystal Vihara
The model Hell-and-Heaven grounds + giant hungry-ghost statues
The pink lotus-petal ordination hall

blocks.name: Wat Khun Inthapramun (Giant Reclining Buddha / Phra Si Mueang Thong)
blocks.area: Inthapramun, Pho Thong District, Ang Thong
blocks.signature: Open-air reclining Buddha around 50 meters long, among the largest in Thailand — an old Sukhothai–Ayutthaya era temple with a pink-leaved bodhi tree
blocks.descHtml:
When it comes to Ang Thong's famous temples, Wat Khun Inthapramun is one of the first names people mention. The star here is the “Phra Buddha Saiyat,” a huge open-air reclining Buddha around 50 meters long and 11 meters high — one of the longest reclining Buddhas in Thailand. It's an ancient monument dating to the Sukhothai period and restored in the Ayutthaya era. Many call the image “Phra Si Mueang Thong,” or simply the reclining Luang Pho. The Buddha reclines across open ground on more than 58 rai, with a gently smiling, serene face that genuinely inspires faith. It suits merit-makers, wish-makers, and anyone drawn to old temples with a story.

The thing not to miss is walking to the soles of the feet to pay respects and apply gold leaf — people traditionally pray here for good health and fortune. Another point everyone talks about is the new three-story ordination hall, built at a cost in the hundreds of millions of baht and fitted with an elevator and escalator, so elderly visitors or anyone with limited mobility can comfortably reach the upper floors to pay respects. Inside are beautifully detailed murals, while around the grounds you'll find an old chedi, the ruins of the Luang Pho Khao vihara, and wax figures of revered monks. Villagers often set up stalls in the temple courtyard selling vegetables, fruit, duck eggs and local snacks — a pleasant browse.

Entry is free with no admission fee, and there's plenty of parking. The temple sits in Inthapramun, Pho Thong District, not far from Ang Thong town — drive along the Ang Thong–Pho Thong highway and the turn-off into the temple is easy. It's open daily from around 6 a.m. until evening. Since the reclining Buddha lies out in the open, mornings or late afternoons into evening are the most comfortable times; the midday sun is fairly harsh and the grounds are wide open.

Worth knowing: this is a sacred temple that draws merit-makers from across the province and its neighbors. Its Google rating runs as high as 4.7 from thousands of reviewers — a sign people leave genuinely impressed. Dress modestly since it's temple grounds, and don't worry about bringing elderly relatives: the walkways are mostly flat, with water and snack stalls to rest at along the way. A very worthwhile stop on any Ang Thong trip.
mustOrder: Pay respects to the 50-meter open-air reclining Buddha
Go up the high-tech 3-story ordination hall and see the murals
Apply gold leaf at the soles of the feet for health and fortune
Browse the community market in the temple grounds for local snacks

blocks.name: Wat Pa Mok Worawihan (The Talking Reclining Buddha)
blocks.signature: Sukhothai-era stucco reclining Buddha around 22.58 m long beside the Chao Phraya River, the legend of the 'talking reclining Buddha', shady old-temple atmosphere
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Pa Mok Worawihan is an old temple on the Chao Phraya River in Pa Mok town — a royal monastery that has stood alongside Ang Thong since the Ayutthaya era. The highlight everyone comes to see is the “Phra Buddha Saiyat,” a large stucco reclining Buddha around 22.58 meters long, lacquered and gilded over the entire figure. It's a remarkably beautiful piece of ancient Buddhist art, reclining on the right side in the lion's posture with a full, serene face. It suits merit-makers wanting the blessings of a reclining Buddha — especially those born on a Tuesday — and anyone who enjoys old temples with legends to tell.

Beyond the Buddha itself, what you shouldn't miss are the two legends that make this temple special. The first is the “moving the Buddha from the water” story: in the reign of King Thai Sa, the image was carefully hauled some 168 meters back from a riverbank being eroded by the current to its present vihara. The second is the legend of the “talking reclining Buddha,” passed down as the tale of a voice from the image reciting a formula for healing medicine. Step into the vihara and the atmosphere feels charged with age. Craft lovers should also see the boat-shaped ordination hall with its gently curved late-Ayutthaya roofline and the old murals, including a painting of a golden mango tree by the hand of Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn.

The temple grounds are shady, quiet and peaceful. Real reviews consistently say mornings are uncrowded and easy for a relaxed visit, and what many appreciate is that nobody presses you for donations — give exactly as much as you wish. There's a large parking lot and no entry fee, so budget only for merit-making and gold leaf. It sits in the Pa Mok municipal area on the Chao Phraya, not far from Ang Thong town, and pairs well with a one-day reclining-Buddha loop through Ang Thong and Sing Buri. Open around 08:00–17:00 daily.

The temple is popular because it combines everything — a beautiful reclining Buddha, legends that are fun to retell, and genuine historical value as an old temple. Its Google rating touches 4.6 from over a thousand reviews. Worth knowing: it's a temple, so dress modestly and remove your shoes before entering the vihara. In early October there's usually the traditional gold-leaf festival for the reclining Buddha, when crowds swell — if you prefer quiet, steer clear of the fair days.
mustOrder: The 22.58 m lacquered-and-gilded stucco reclining Buddha
The legends of the talking reclining Buddha + moving the Buddha from the water
The boat-shaped ordination hall + late-Ayutthaya murals
The golden mango tree painted by Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn

blocks.name: Ban Hun Lek Ang Thong (Iron Robot House)
blocks.area: Talat Kruat, Mueang Ang Thong District
blocks.signature: Sculptures welded from scrap metal and car parts — robots, superheroes, sports cars, motorbikes — plus a cafe and a noodle shop; entry ฿60 adults, ฿30 kids
blocks.priceRange: Adults ฿60 · Kids ฿30 · Children under 90 cm free
blocks.descHtml:
Ban Hun Lek is a homegrown Thai theme park born from the passion of craftsman Phairot Thanomwong, who welds scrap metal and old car parts into robots and superheroes ranging from life-size up to several meters tall — Transformers, Iron Man, Captain America, Batman, Gundam, Alien, Predator — plus sports cars and motorbikes shaped entirely from steel. It suits families with kids, superhero movie and comic fans, and anyone driving the Asia Highway who fancies a fun hour-long photo stop.

The unmissable highlight is the giant robots towering into view before you even reach the gate. Inside, the grounds split into Indoor and Outdoor zones with hundreds of figures to photograph, a Thai-house corner with a Ganesha and Buddha images crafted from steel, a kids' playground, and a workshop zone where you can watch the builders assembling figures live. When you need a break, the air-conditioned “Sapha Kafae” coffee shop draws mentions in many reviews for its “Sweet Rust” menu item made from chocolate and its French rose tea; there's also a noodle shop and a souvenir store on site.

Admission is easy on the wallet: adults 60 baht, kids 30 baht, children under 90 cm tall free. Open daily 09:00–17:00, located at 41/2 Mu 6, Talat Kruat, Mueang Ang Thong District, right on the Asia Highway (Highway 32) on the Bangkok-bound side, about a two-hour drive from the capital. Parking is easy and it makes a convenient stop en route. Most visitors spend around 40 minutes to 1–2 hours, depending on how thoroughly they browse.

Ban Hun Lek keeps growing in fame — international media have even featured it — partly because it's a recycling idea that turns discarded material into something valuable, and every corner photographs well. The owner has since expanded the grounds from 3 rai to 6 rai, added roofing, installed cooling mist sprayers, and made the paths wheelchair-accessible. One small heads-up from real reviews: some spots still carry the smell of spray paint, so bring a mask if you're sensitive to fumes, and since the midday sun is strong, plan the outdoor zones for morning or late afternoon.
mustOrder: Photograph the giant Transformers/Iron Man/Predator figures in both Indoor and Outdoor zones
Watch craftsmen assembling figures from real scrap metal in the workshop
Rest in the air-conditioned Sapha Kafae — try the 'Sweet Rust' (chocolate) and French rose tea
Visit the Thai-house Buddha corner and the playground for little kids

blocks.bestFor: Families with kids, robot and superhero fans, and anyone after a photo stop on the Asia Highway heading back to Bangkok

blocks.name: Wat Tha It (Phra That Chedi Si Pho Thong)
blocks.signature: Golden octagonal chedi around 73 m tall — climb to the upper level for views over Ang Thong, with Wat Muang's Big Buddha visible; Lanka–Ayutthaya–Rattanakosin art
blocks.priceRange: Free entry · parking inside the temple grounds
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Tha It in Bang Phlap, Pho Thong District, is the temple where a huge, gleaming golden chedi catches your eye the moment you drive in. That's the “Phra That Chedi Si Pho Thong,” a golden octagonal chedi around 73 meters tall and 40 meters wide blending Lanka, Ayutthaya and Rattanakosin styles, built during the abbotship of Luang Pho Hom to enshrine a relic of the Buddha's neck. It suits merit-makers who want a beautiful temple not far from Bangkok and photographers after a corner that isn't crowded yet — if you like quiet temples where you never have to fight for a frame, you'll love it here.

The unmissable part is climbing up inside the chedi level by level — each floor holds Buddha images in different postures to pay respects to — until you reach the top for the view. Real reviews agree that from the summit you get a 360-degree panorama of Ang Thong's rice fields, and on a clear day you can just make out the Big Buddha over at Wat Muang. Many say the chedi is spectacular and its gold strikingly beautiful, though they also warn the climb is fairly steep and tiring — if your knees aren't great, take it slowly and rest in stages.

Budget-wise it couldn't be easier: entry is free, there's parking inside the temple, and the temple provides drinking water. It sits along Highway 3064 around kilometer 7–8, about 1–2 kilometers before Pho Thong Hospital, a short drive from Ang Thong town. Open around 08:00–18:00 daily; under an hour covers it all, making it a handy stop between other temples on an Ang Thong merit-making run.

Worth a small note: some reviews mention that parts of the chedi interior are dusty and look a little under-maintained — it isn't polished spotless at all times — but the calm and the view from the top still make the stop worthwhile. This isn't a temple packed with tourists, so you get a quiet, private atmosphere. If you're the merit-making, spiritually inclined type who also loves photographing beautiful golden chedis, you'll come away with both — and whatever you do, climb all the way to the top for the rice-field view many call the temple's highlight.
mustOrder: Climb the octagonal chedi to the top floor for a 360-degree view of Ang Thong's rice fields
Pay respects to the Buddha's neck relic + the Buddha images on each floor
Photograph the gleaming 73-meter golden Si Pho Thong chedi
Spot Wat Muang's Big Buddha from the top on a clear day

blocks.title: 🛏️ Places to Stay in Ang Thong
blocks.text: If you'd rather explore Ang Thong without rushing the drive back, consider staying a night in town or near the Chao Phraya River. There are small hotels, riverside resorts and friendly-priced guesthouses in good locations close to the main sights, so you can wake up and keep temple-hopping. Booking ahead through an app gets you better rates and first pick of the rooms with a view.

blocks.name: San Chao Rong Thong Market (Wiset Chai Chan 100-Year Market)
blocks.area: San Chao Rong Thong, Wiset Chai Chan District
blocks.signature: Century-old market of Thai-Chinese wooden shophouses in long rows — traditional Thai sweets, boat noodles, community food and souvenirs; open around 08:00–16:00
blocks.descHtml:
San Chao Rong Thong Market — better known as the Wiset Chai Chan 100-year market — is an old market on the Noi River where Teochew Chinese settlers put down roots around B.E. 2420 (1877). Its signature is the long rows of Thai-Chinese wooden shophouses lining both sides of the walkway, built so close together you can wander through without the heat, and it never feels overly crowded. It suits fans of nostalgic old markets, hunters of hard-to-find traditional Thai sweets, and families bringing older relatives for a relaxed stroll. The market won an outstanding architectural conservation award in 2007 after the community pulled together to restore it following a major fire, keeping the charm of the old wooden houses fully intact.

The unmissable highlight is the traditional Thai sweets you can rarely find elsewhere — above all khanom kesorn lamjiak, considered Ang Thong's signature provincial sweet — along with old-recipe charcoal-stove ba-bin, khanom khi khwai, khanom sommanat, and shrimp-topped khanom krok. Shops people mention often are Song Nimit, which sells many kinds of traditional sweets and once won an award for preserving Thai desserts, and the charcoal-brewed traditional coffee shop using the market's age-old recipe. For a proper meal there are noodles and savory dishes to sit down to. Most things are inexpensive, so you can graze your way along all day without straining your wallet.

Budget-wise it's easy: the market has no entry fee, and you can wander the old wooden houses and take photos for free, paying only for the snacks you want to try. It sits in the Wiset Chai Chan municipal area on the Noi River, near Wat Nang Nai and the Guan Yu shrine. Open daily around 08:00–16:00, with parking across from the market and along the road near the temple. It's a short drive from Ang Thong town — a great grazing-and-strolling stop on any Ang Thong itinerary.

A small tip: the market is at its liveliest on Saturday, Sunday and public-holiday mornings, when the most vendors come out; on weekdays some shops may close or carry less stock. Some of the traditional sweets are made fresh and sell out fast, so come in the morning if you want the full selection. Allow 1–2 hours to stroll the wooden houses, sample the sweets, and visit the shrines in the same neighborhood.
mustOrder: Khanom kesorn lamjiak — Ang Thong's signature provincial sweet
Old-recipe charcoal-stove ba-bin
Traditional charcoal-brewed coffee, old recipe
Stroll the century-old Thai-Chinese wooden shophouses for retro photos

blocks.name: Wat Chaiyo Worawihan (Luang Pho To / Phra Maha Phuttha Phim)
blocks.signature: Phra Maha Phuttha Phim, 'Luang Pho To' — a huge seated stucco Buddha inside a soaring vihara; an old royal temple tied to Somdet Phra Phutthachan (To Phrommarangsi)
blocks.descHtml:
If you want to pay respects to a Buddha so vast you clutch your chest just looking up at it, Wat Chaiyo Worawihan — or “Wat Ket Chaiyo,” as locals call it — is a pin you can't skip on an Ang Thong trip. The highlight is “Phra Maha Phuttha Phim,” or “Luang Pho To,” a colossal stucco Buddha in the meditation posture enshrined inside a vihara that soars beside the Chao Phraya River. The image was created by Somdet Phra Phutthachan (To Phrommarangsi), and after a major restoration in the reign of King Rama V it received its royal name and the temple was elevated to a second-class royal monastery. If you follow the Somdet To tradition, or simply love old temples with long stories to tell, you'll leave here with a full heart.

The must-dos are paying respects to Luang Pho To in the vihara, then walking on to the ordination hall for its murals of the Buddha's life by Rama V-era craftsmen — so beautiful that many reviewers say they deserve a slow, careful look. If you enjoy relaxed merit-making, you can feed the fish at the pier in front of the temple; on some evenings around 5 p.m. the monks come to feed the fish and lift big ones out of the water for a close-up look, a scene kids adore. Around the temple there's also the “Talat Tong Chom” riverside market, where vendors dressed in traditional sabai sell local goods and Thai sweets — make merit, then eat well right after.

The overall atmosphere is shady, quiet and cooled by the river breeze. Reviews agree the temple is clean and easy to walk around, with free parking and no entry fee — just bring money for merit-making and a few souvenirs. One small observation: the temple courtyard is quite open, and the midday sun is strong, so packing an umbrella or hat keeps things comfortable — and dress modestly, since this is an important temple with a steady stream of worshippers.

It sits in Chaiyo, Chaiyo District, about 18 kilometers from Ang Thong town on the Ang Thong–Sing Buri road, on the west bank of the Chao Phraya. Open daily roughly 07:00–17:00. Its popularity comes from being an old royal temple tied directly to Somdet To — the famed “Somdet Ket Chaiyo” amulets carry the name — plus the giant Buddha in its tall vihara, the riverside market and the fish feeding, so a single visit delivers merit, views and good food all at once. Great for both the devout and families wanting an easygoing riverside temple day near Bangkok.
mustOrder: Pay respects to Luang Pho To (Phra Maha Phuttha Phim) in the soaring vihara
See the Rama V-era murals of the Buddha's life in the ordination hall
Feed the fish at the pier in front of the temple
Stroll the Talat Tong Chom market on the Chao Phraya

blocks.name: Wat Sang Kratai (The Bodhi-Wrapped Chapel)
blocks.area: Sala Daeng, Mueang Ang Thong District
blocks.signature: An old Ayutthaya-era ordination hall completely embraced by the roots of giant bodhi trees — hauntingly atmospheric, Ang Thong's unseen-vibe photo spot
blocks.descHtml:
When it comes to Ang Thong's “unseen” attractions, Wat Sang Kratai always comes up first. It's an abandoned ancient site in Sala Daeng, about 7 kilometers west of town — just a ten-minute drive. What draws people here is the 400-plus-year-old Ayutthaya-era ordination hall, of which only three roofless chambers of walls remain, now gripped tight on all four sides by the creeping roots of four great bodhi trees. The result is an image of trees cradling a chapel, so hauntingly atmospheric that many rank it a highlight of the province. It suits moody-photography fans, lovers of ancient ruins, and the spiritually minded who want to pay respects to old Buddha images in a tranquil setting.

The must-do is circling the hall to watch how the bodhi roots drape the walls, as if nature itself were holding the old building up. Inside are four Buddha images — Luang Pho Kaen in the first chamber; Luang Pho Wan Di, Luang Pho Si and Luang Pho Suk in the middle; and the hermit figure Pho Pu Ruesi in the last — so those drawn to the sacred can come to pray and make wishes. Another point of distinction: the bodhi trees surrounding the chapel were registered as national heritage trees (“Rukkha Moradok of the Land”) in 2017. Most real reviews agree the atmosphere is quiet, shaded and unlike any ordinary temple.

The site is open around 08:00–17:00 daily, free of charge, with only donation boxes for those who wish to give. There's a fair amount of parking, and it's an easy drive from Ang Thong town via the Pho Phraya–Tha Ruea road — just pin “Wat Sang Kratai” on Google Maps. It's often slotted in as a stop alongside Ang Thong's famous temples on a one-day loop.

Before you go: the chapel is ancient and the roots fragile, so walk gently — no climbing, no tugging at the roots — and dress modestly, as this is a sacred place. Early morning and late afternoon bring soft light and fewer people, far better for photos than midday. Pack an umbrella or hat for the sun, and leave a little time to sit and soak up the stillness — you'll understand why this place is on every Ang Thong must-visit list.
mustOrder: See the roots of 4 bodhi trees embracing the old ordination hall on all four sides
Pay respects to the 4 principal Buddha images in the 3 chambers (Luang Pho Kaen/Wan Di/Si/Suk) and Pho Pu Ruesi
Capture the root-draped walls — Ang Thong's signature atmospheric photo spot
See the national heritage tree plaque (registered 2017)

blocks.name: Ekkarat Drum-Making Village (Ban Bang Phae)
blocks.area: Ekkarat, Pa Mok District, Ang Thong
blocks.signature: Thailand's biggest and best-known drum-making village — watch every step from lathing the wood to stretching the hide and tuning, with a giant drum as the photo spot
blocks.descHtml:
If you're driving the Ang Thong–Ayutthaya road through Pa Mok and spot an enormous drum displayed by the roadside, that's the Ekkarat drum-making village — Ban Bang Phae to the old-timers — a community that has been making and selling drums since around 1927, earning its reputation as the biggest and most famous drum-making source in Thailand. Walk into the lane and you'll find dozens of craftsmen's houses in a row, each open for a casual, friendly wander. It suits craft lovers, parents who want their kids to see genuine folk knowledge at work, and anyone who simply needs to stretch their legs on the way to Ayutthaya.

The highlight is watching every step happen live — lathing rain-tree logs hollow, stretching cowhide over the drumhead, hammering in the wooden pegs, then tuning by ear right on the spot. Every kind of drum is on show: klong that, klong yao, ramwong drums, temple klong phen, all the way down to miniature souvenir drums. Don't miss the village's giant landmark drum — its head nearly a meter across and the body several meters long, joined from multiple rain-tree logs — everyone lines up beside it for a scale shot. What impresses many visitors is that the craftsmen here also make international drums for export, from Japanese taiko to Korean janggu and samba drums.

Budget is no issue, since visiting is free for kids and adults alike. There's parking, and you're welcome to browse and chat with the makers whether you buy or not. Open daily around 08:00–17:00, but come late morning to afternoon if you want to see the craftsmen actually at work. The village is in Ekkarat, Pa Mok District, behind Pa Mok market, not far from either Ang Thong town or Ayutthaya — driving yourself is easiest. One small note: online reviews are fewer than the place deserves, since it's more a community learning site than a mainstream check-in spot, but visitors who come and watch the makers at work usually leave impressed — it's a sight that's hard to find anywhere else in Thailand now.
mustOrder: Watch craftsmen lathe the wood, stretch cowhide, set pegs and tune drums live
Photograph the giant klong yao/temple drum — the village landmark
Shop drums of every size, from mini souvenirs to temple drums
Check out the export drums — Japanese taiko, Korean janggu, samba drums

blocks.name: Kham Yat Palace (Phra Tamnak Kham Yat)
blocks.area: Kham Yat, Pho Thong District, Ang Thong
blocks.signature: A brick-and-stucco palace standing alone in wide fields — a late-Ayutthaya monument linked to Prince Uthumphon ('Khun Luang Ha Wat'), with stucco reliefs on the doorway and window arches
blocks.descHtml:
If you like quiet places with long stories hidden inside, Phra Tamnak Kham Yat should suit you. This is the ruin of a brick-and-stucco palace standing alone amid wide rice fields in Kham Yat, Pho Thong District — a late-Ayutthaya monument linked to King Uthumphon, better known as “Khun Luang Ha Wat,” the monarch who abdicated to enter the monkhood and retreated to these parts. The building measures roughly 10 by 20 meters; today only the four walls remain and the roof structure is long gone, yet the outlines of its original beauty are still clearly visible. It suits history lovers, photographers of ancient monuments, and anyone wanting to escape the noise into stillness.

The highlight not to miss is the stucco work on the doorway arches and window frames. The door and window openings are pointed arches in the style popular since the reign of King Narai, showing Persian artistic influence — look closely and you can still trace the old craftsmen's handiwork on the brick walls. Another angle many people love is stepping back to frame the whole palace against green rice fields and open sky — a simple shot with quiet charm. Morning and evening light is soft; many real reviews say the atmosphere is profoundly calm, quiet enough to hear the wind, and some joke that the place now belongs to its resident flock of pigeons.

Costs are easy on the wallet: entry is free with no ticket, and it's an open-air site within the grounds of an abandoned temple, accessible all day. Midday to evening shows the details most clearly and photographs best. It's in Pho Thong District, a short drive from Ang Thong town — an easy add-on to a temple-hopping day in the province, with easy road access and roadside parking.

People come because this counts among Ang Thong's important historic monuments, registered by the Fine Arts Department, valuable both for its story and its solemn beauty. Know before you go: it's a roofless ruin in open fields with nothing to block the sun — bring a hat or umbrella, sunscreen and water. The surrounding ground is dirt and grass, so comfortable walking shoes are better. Help keep the site clean and don't climb the old walls, so this place can stand for many more years.
mustOrder: The stucco reliefs on the doorway and window frames
Pointed-arch doorways and windows in the King Narai-era style
The shot of the palace framed against the rice fields
The story of Khun Luang Ha Wat — Prince Uthumphon

blocks.title: Book Ang Thong Tours and Tickets in Advance
blocks.text: Ang Thong's sights are spread across several districts. If you'd rather not drive — or you're traveling as a group — booking a guided temple tour through Klook or GetYourGuide keeps the trip running smoothly with no route-planning needed. Some packages include round-trip transfers from Bangkok and cover several stops in a single day, ideal if you'd rather sit back and let a local lead the way. Compare packages and book tickets ahead — it's better value and saves you queuing time.

blocks.title: Know Before You Go: Ang Thong

items.title: Renting a car or booking a tour is easiest
items.text: The sights are spread across several districts and public transport within the province is scarce. Driving yourself, or hiring a car with a driver from Bangkok, is the most convenient option. Grab cars are hard to find in Ang Thong town — don't rely on it as your main transport.

items.title: Always carry cash
items.text: Temple merit-making, donation boxes, the century-old market and most local sweet shops take cash only. Keep small notes and coins on hand. ATMs exist in town, but they're hard to find at temples outside it.

items.title: Go early to beat the sun and the queues
items.text: Many of the big Buddhas and reclining Buddhas sit in the open, and the midday sun is fierce. Morning to late morning is far more comfortable for walking and photos, with fewer people. Long weekends and festivals get crowded — allow extra time for parking.

items.title: Dress modestly for temples
items.text: This is a merit-making destination. Dress neatly, cover shoulders and knees inside temple grounds and ordination halls, and remove your shoes before entering a vihara — etiquette locals take seriously.

items.title: English is limited
items.text: Ang Thong is a second-tier town visited mainly by Thais, so English signs and menus are scarce. Carry a translation app and save the temple names in Thai script for asking directions — it helps a lot. Locals are kind and happy to help.

items.title: Signature souvenirs: drums and Thai sweets
items.text: Stop by the Ekkarat drum-making village to watch drums being made and pick up a miniature drum as a keepsake, while San Chao Rong Thong Market has traditional Thai sweets and community foods to take home. Sweets run about ฿20–60 — have cash ready to shop.

blocks.title: How to Plan a Worthwhile One-Day Ang Thong Trip
blocks.html:
Ang Thong is ideal for a day trip from Bangkok because the sights cluster in just a few districts, so routing by zone saves the most time. Start the morning on the Wiset Chai Chan side at Wat Muang (Luang Pho Yai), then stop at San Chao Rong Thong Market for traditional Thai sweets by the Noi River as a late-morning bite. Next cross to the Pho Thong zone for Wat Khun Inthapramun (the reclining Buddha), Wat Tha It (climb the golden chedi for the view) and Kham Yat Palace, all close together. In the afternoon loop into town for Ban Hun Lek and Wat Sang Kratai, then finish on the Pa Mok–Chaiyo side with Wat Pa Mok, Wat Chaiyo Worawihan and the Ekkarat drum-making village.

Nearly every temple is free to enter, with donations as you wish. The one paid stop is Ban Hun Lek: adults 60 baht, kids 30 baht, children under 90 cm free. Ang Thong's temples generally open for open-air worship from morning to evening, while San Chao Rong Thong Market is lively from morning to afternoon, around 08:00–16:00 — go before noon for the full food selection. The sun here is strong and many of the big Buddhas sit in the open, so bring an umbrella, hat and drinking water and you'll be far more comfortable.

blocks.text: After a day covering Ang Thong's sights, skip the late-night drive back to Bangkok — check out well-located places to stay in town and near the river first. Prices are friendly, and booking ahead gets you the better rooms.

faq.q: What are the can't-miss spots in Ang Thong?
faq.a: The two you absolutely must see are Wat Muang in Wiset Chai Chan District, home of Luang Pho Yai (Phra Buddha Maha Nawamin Sakyamuni Sri Wiset Chai Chan) — Thailand's largest seated Buddha at around 63 meters across the lap and around 95 meters tall, gleaming gold amid the rice fields — and Wat Khun Inthapramun in Pho Thong District, with its open-air reclining Buddha around 50 meters long. These two are the icons of the province that nearly every visitor to Ang Thong stops at.

faq.q: What are Ang Thong's highlights besides temples?
faq.a: Beyond beautiful temples and giant Buddhas, Ang Thong has plenty of quirkier stops: Ban Hun Lek in town, where robots and superheroes are built from scrap metal and car parts, complete with a cafe and noodle shop; the Ekkarat drum-making village in Pa Mok, where you can watch every step of drum-making; Wat Sang Kratai, whose old ordination hall is wrapped whole in bodhi-tree roots; and Kham Yat Palace, a late-Ayutthaya monument standing in the middle of the fields.

faq.q: Do Ang Thong's attractions charge entry fees?
faq.a: Nearly every temple on this list is free to enter, with donations or the donation box entirely up to you — Wat Muang, Wat Khun Inthapramun, Wat Pa Mok, Wat Tha It, Wat Chaiyo and Wat Sang Kratai — and Kham Yat Palace and the Ekkarat drum-making village are also free to visit. The one paid stop is Ban Hun Lek: adults 60 baht, kids 30 baht, children under 90 cm free. San Chao Rong Thong Market is free to stroll — you only pay for the snacks.

faq.q: How do I get to Ang Thong, and what's parking like?
faq.a: The most convenient way is driving your own or a rented car from Bangkok, taking about an hour and a half to two hours, since the sights are spread across several districts — Wiset Chai Chan, Pho Thong, Mueang, Pa Mok and Chaiyo. Most temples and attractions have their own spacious free parking. Without a car, vans and coaches run from Bangkok to Ang Thong town, from where local hire cars or motorbike taxis reach each spot — workable, but less convenient than driving yourself.

faq.q: What time do Ang Thong's attractions open?
faq.a: The temples generally open for open-air worship from morning to evening every day; morning to mid-afternoon is the best window. Ban Hun Lek opens around 09:00–17:00 daily, while San Chao Rong Thong Market is lively around 08:00–16:00 — go before noon for the full food selection. Many of the big Buddhas sit in the open and the sun is strong, so avoiding high noon makes the walk much easier.
